screens.title: What is a logical backup?
screens.narratorSegment: A logical backup captures database objects and their data as S Q L statements or as logical archive files that map schema and rows, rather than copying low-level database files. The key benefit is portability: logical backups can be restored across minor and sometimes major PostgreSQL versions, inspected in a text editor, and selectively applied. For example, a plain S Q L dump shows CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements, which you can read to audit schema changes. However, logical backups can be slower for very large data sets and may require different strategies for performance. A common misconception is that logical backups replace physical backups — they do not. Physical backups capture the exact on-disk state and are required for point-in-time recovery. Use logical backups when you need portability, auditing, selective restores, or schema migration. As a practical rule, combine logical and physical backups in your strategy: logical for portability and selective needs, and physical for fast full recovery and point-in-time requirements. Consider the restore path when you select a logical format so you always know how recovery will proceed.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a logical backup?
Definition

Logical backup explained

  • Exports schema and data as SQL statements or logical archive files.
  • Portable across servers and readable for audits or migrations.
  • Enables selective restore of tables or schemas when using archive formats.
  • Not a drop-in replacement for physical backups required for point-in-time recovery.
Example
A plain SQL dump contains CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements that you can inspect and edit before restoring with psql.
pg_dump -U postgres mydatabase > mydatabase_backup.sql
Why it matters

Logical backups let you move schema and data between systems and perform migrations with visibility into SQL statements. They are ideal for audits and selective recovery but should be paired with physical backups for a complete recovery plan.

Key Takeaway

Logical backups are portable and inspectable; choose format based on recovery and performance needs.

Common mistake

Assuming a logical dump is sufficient for point-in-time recovery; it is not a replacement for physical backups.

screens.title: Using pg_dump: basic commands
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the basic pg_dump invocation and what each part does. A typical simple command is pg_dump -U postgres mydatabase > mydatabase_backup. sql. The -U option specifies the user for the connection; depending on your authentication method you may be prompted for a password. The database name tells pg_dump which single database to export; remember pg_dump operates per database and will not export cluster-level objects. The greater-than symbol redirects the standard output of pg_dump into a file. This plain-text S Q L script contains CREATE and INSERT or COPY statements and is easily inspected and edited. Use this form for small databases or when you need to audit schema changes. A misconception is thinking redirection always creates a portable binary; it produces a readable S Q L file and may be slow for very large datasets. If you need parallel restores or selective object recovery later, prefer custom or directory formats. Practice: create a small sample database, run the command, open the produced S Q L script, and confirm the presence of CREATE statements. This exercise reinforces what is captured and how you would restore it using psql.

Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › pg_dump Basics
Code Walkthrough

Plain-text SQL dump

A readable script suitable for small databases and audits.

pg_dump -U postgres mydatabase > mydatabase_backup.sql
Check the file to see CREATE TABLE and INSERT or COPY statements that recreate schema and data.
Key points
  • -U specifies the connection user; authentication still applies.
  • Redirection writes standard output to a file you can restore with psql.
  • pg_dump backs up one database only; global objects are not included.
Pro tip

Use plain format for small test databases and audits, not for large production restores.

screens.title: pg_dump output formats
screens.narratorSegment: pg_dump supports multiple output formats, and choosing the right one affects your restore options and performance. The plain text format produces a S Q L script and is easy to inspect and edit, making it useful for audits or cross-version compatibility. The custom format is compressed and flexible; it is the recommended general-purpose format because pg_restore can selectively restore objects and run multiple jobs in parallel. Tar format creates an archive similar to custom but is slightly less flexible; you can still extract components with pg_restore. The directory format generates a directory with one file per table and a table-of-contents file. Directory format shines on very large databases because you can dump and restore in parallel using --jobs. A common mistake is using plain format for large datasets; restoring becomes slow and stressful. If you expect to restore specific tables or benefit from parallelism, choose custom (-F c) or directory (-F d). For small databases or when you must hand-edit S Q L, plain format remains appropriate. Consider your restore scenarios when picking a format so backups match your recovery needs.

keyIdea.title: Format choice
keyIdea.text: Select format based on inspectability, selective restore needs, and parallelism requirements: plain, custom, tar, or directory.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Output Formats
Comparison

Plain vs Custom vs Tar vs Directory

Plain (default)
SQL script, human-readable, easy to inspect. Use for small DBs or audits.
Custom (-F c)
Compressed archive, flexible for selective restore with pg_restore and parallel restore support.
Tar (-F t)
Tar archive with separate files per object; somewhat less flexible than custom but usable with pg_restore.
Directory (-F d)
Directory with one file per table and a TOC; excellent for parallel dumps and restores using --jobs.
When to pick custom

Choose custom for selective restore, compressed storage, and good cross-version behavior with pg_restore tools.

When to pick directory

Use directory for very large databases where parallelism across many jobs significantly speeds up dumps and restores.

screens.title: Custom and directory formats in practice
screens.narratorSegment: Custom and directory formats unlock selective restore and parallelism. Create a custom archive with pg_dump -F c -f mydb. custom mydatabase. This file is compressed and contains a table of contents that pg_restore can read. To restore a custom archive, use pg_restore and you can select specific tables or schema elements, and specify parallel jobs where supported. The directory format uses -F d and writes a folder with one file per table plus a TOC file; this layout is ideal for running pg_dump or pg_restore with --jobs to exploit multiple CPUs. For example, use pg_dump -F d -f /tmp/mydb_dir mydatabase and later pg_restore -j 4 -d targetdb /tmp/mydb_dir to restore using four jobs. A common misconception is that --jobs speeds up plain S Q L dumps — it does not; parallel jobs work only with custom and directory formats. When dealing with very large tables, the directory format may simplify partial recovery because individual table files are separate. Always test restores locally to confirm that parallel restore orders and dependency resolutions succeed, and remember that pg_dump with jobs reduces wall-clock time but still requires sufficient input and output throughput.

keyIdea.text: Use -F c or -F d and pg_restore with --jobs to enable selective and parallel restore; plain format does not support parallel jobs.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Custom & Directory
Create
pg_dump -U postgres -F c -f /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump sales_db
pg_dump -U postgres -F d -f /tmp/sales_db_dir sales_db
Custom is a single compressed archive. Directory is a folder structure with separate files for each table and a TOC file.
Restore
pg_restore -U postgres -d targetdb /tmp/sales_db_custom.dump
pg_restore -U postgres -j 4 -d targetdb /tmp/sales_db_dir
Use -j with custom or directory formats to restore in parallel. Test restores to ensure dependencies resolve in your target environment.
Key Takeaway

Custom or directory formats give you the flexibility and speed needed for large datasets and selective recovery.

Pitfall

Expect lower wall-clock time with jobs but ensure your storage I/O can sustain parallel operations.

screens.title: pg_dump options to control content
screens.narratorSegment: pg_dump includes many options to control which parts of a database you export. --schema-only produces only DDL statements such as CREATE TABLE and CREATE INDEX, which is useful when migrating schema or creating a development environment without data. --data-only exports table data without DDL; this is valuable when you already have the schema in place and need to populate data. --clean adds DROP commands before CREATE statements so restores can start from a clean state; --create includes a CREATE DATABASE statement so the dump can recreate the database itself. The --inserts and --column-inserts options force insertion via INSERT statements rather than COPY; these are safer for older server compatibility or differing column orders but are much slower. Use --exclude-table or --exclude-schema to omit parts of the database you don't want included. A common misconception is that --data-only will always restore faster — performance depends on method: COPY is usually faster than INSERT. Choose options based on the restore scenario: schema migrations, data refreshes, or selective table transfers. Practice by creating schema-only and data-only dumps and restoring them to a prepared target to confirm behavior.

keyIdea.title: Control options
keyIdea.text: Use pg_dump options to target schema, data, or tune restore behavior; select flags based on the intended restore workflow.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › pg_dump Options
Options
  • --schema-only: dump DDL only.
  • --data-only: dump table data without DDL.
  • --clean: include DROP statements before CREATE.
  • --create: include CREATE DATABASE for full recreate.
  • --inserts / --column-inserts: dump using INSERT statements.
  • --exclude-table / --exclude-schema: omit patterns from the dump.
Examples
pg_dump -U postgres --schema-only sales_db > sales_schema.sql
pg_dump -U postgres --data-only sales_db > sales_data.sql
pg_dump -U postgres --exclude-table=logs_* -F c -f /tmp/sales_custom.dump sales_db
Test schema-only restore to ensure procedural code and extensions are available before loading data-only dumps.
Pro tip

When migrating schema, restore schema-only first, verify extensions and privileges, then load data-only dumps.

Misconception

Using --inserts slows restore significantly; prefer COPY where performance matters.

screens.title: What pg_dump does not include
screens.narratorSegment: It’s important to understand the limits of pg_dump: it backs up a single database’s schema and data but does not capture cluster-wide global objects. Global objects include roles (users), tablespaces, and database definitions themselves. If you only back up individual databases with pg_dump, you may miss role definitions and tablespace definitions that are required when restoring into a new instance. This omission can cause restore failures or require manual re-creation of those objects. To capture global objects, use pg_dumpall, which outputs a plain-text S Q L script that contains CREATE ROLE and CREATE TABLESPACE statements followed by per-database dumps. A common mistake is relying solely on pg_dump archives and neglecting roles; after a crash, restoring databases without recreating roles can leave ownership and privileges broken. Therefore, include a pg_dumpall export in your backup plan for cluster metadata. For selective restores, still rely on per-database pg_dump archives, but keep a recent pg_dumpall for global state so you can reconstitute the instance accurately in disaster recovery. What pg_dump does not include means pg_dump omits cluster global objects; use pg_dumpall to capture roles, tablespaces, and database definitions for full instance recovery.. In practical terms, global objects and why pg_dumpall is necessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Limits of pg_dump
Definition

Global objects are not in pg_dump

  • Roles and users (CREATE ROLE statements)
  • Tablespaces (CREATE TABLESPACE statements)
  • Database definitions (CREATE DATABASE statements)

pg_dump focuses on a single database; missing globals must be captured separately for full recovery.

pg_dumpall Example
pg_dumpall -U postgres > full_cluster_backup.sql
This single plain-text file includes global CREATE ROLE and CREATE TABLESPACE statements followed by per-database dumps.
Why it matters

Without a pg_dumpall export, restores may miss critical roles and tablespace configurations, causing operational errors after recovery.

screens.title: Creating a pg_dumpall cluster backup
screens.narratorSegment: pg_dumpall produces a plain-text S Q L script that represents the entire cluster, including global objects. A typical command is pg_dumpall -U postgres > full_cluster_backup. sql. The output begins with CREATE ROLE and CREATE TABLESPACE statements, then includes CREATE DATABASE commands and per-database dumps. This single file is convenient for capturing the full instance state, but it can be large and difficult to edit if you only need a subset of objects. If you must restore specific parts from a pg_dumpall script, you may need to manually extract sections, which is error-prone. The recommended approach is to keep per-database pg_dump archives for recovery of individual databases, and maintain a pg_dumpall export to capture the global configuration that pg_dump omits. During recovery, restore the pg_dumpall script first to recreate roles and tablespaces, then restore individual database archives. A common misconception is that pg_dumpall replaces per-database backups — it does not. Plan your backup sequence and test it in a staging environment to validate the order and completeness of restores. Creating a pg_dumpall cluster backup means pg_dumpall captures cluster-level global objects in a single plain-text sql script; restore it before individual database archives for full recovery.. In practical terms, capture global objects and full cluster state into a single script. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Backups are only useful if stored safely and validated regularly. Place backup files on a separate disk or, preferably, off the primary server on a different machine or cloud storage to protect against disk or server loss. Apply strict file permissions so only a small set of administrators can read or write backup files. Encryption or secure object storage is recommended where sensitive data exists. Importantly, test your backups by performing restores in a separate environment. This validates both the content of the backup and your recovery procedure. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Administrators commonly make avoidable mistakes when creating logical backups. The first frequent error is assuming pg_dump includes global objects; without pg_dumpall you may miss roles and tablespaces. To prevent this, schedule a pg_dumpall alongside per-database pg_dump archives and test restores to ensure roles and ownership map correctly. Second, choosing the wrong format for the use case — using plain format for very large databases — can cause slow restores; choose custom or directory formats for parallelism and selective restores. Third, not testing restores or storing backups on the same server exposes you to single-point failures; always store backups off-host and perform restore drills. Fourth, using --inserts indiscriminately can severely slow restoration; prefer COPY-based dumps unless compatibility requires INSERT statements. Finally, forgetting permissions on backup files can allow unauthorized access; set restrictive permissions and consider encryption. For each mistake, there is a prevention step: include pg_dumpall, choose appropriate formats, store backups off-site, test restores often, and secure backup files. These practices make your backup strategy reliable and actionable when you most need it. fullNarratorScript:
Today we learn how to create reliable logical backups in PostgreSQL using the built-in tools. Logical backups export schema and data into scripts or archives that you can inspect, version, and move between systems. You will understand when to use pg_dump for individual databases and when to use pg_dumpall for capturing cluster-wide objects like roles and tablespaces. For example, use a plain S Q L dump when you want a human-readable script to review, and use the custom or directory formats when you need compressed archives that support parallel restore and selective object recovery. We will also look at options such as schema-only or data-only exports and explain how those options change your workflow during migrations or testing. I’ll point out common mistakes, like assuming pg_dump captures roles, and show a minimal hands-on sequence you can reproduce: create a small database, produce a few formats, inspect the outputs, and run a restore test. By the end you should be able to choose a format for a use case and plan where and how to store backups safely. What backup strategy would you pick for your systems after this overview?

By the end of this chapter you will execute pg_dump to produce logical backups for individual databases and understand how different output formats affect portability and restoration. You will also use pg_dump options to include or exclude schema and data, and to prepare backups suitable for parallel restore. A second objective is to run pg_dumpall so you can capture global objects like roles, tablespaces, and database definitions that pg_dump alone does not include. Additionally, you'll learn how to select the right format for a use case — for instance choosing custom or directory formats for large datasets that need parallelism and selective object recovery, or plain-text for small, auditable dumps. Finally, you will identify common mistakes, such as assuming a single-database dump includes cluster roles, and learn how to avoid them by combining pg_dump backups with a pg_dumpall export. These skills make your backup strategy robust, auditable, and testable.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application and validation. First, you will practice running pg_dump in multiple formats and learn how each format affects restore strategies; for example, using the custom format to restore a single table with pg_restore. Second, you will plan storage and permissions: backups must be on separate storage and protected by permissions to avoid unauthorized access. Third, you will test backups by restoring into a separate environment — this validates both the backup content and your procedures. Finally, you will form a combined strategy: keep per-database pg_dump archives for selective restores and a pg_dumpall plain script for global objects. Each objective pairs a command or configuration with a reason: faster restores, selective recovery, and safe storage. Practice and testing build confidence; a backup that you cannot restore is not a backup. After these steps you should be ready to implement a repeatable backup and restore workflow.

A logical backup captures database objects and their data as S Q L statements or as logical archive files that map schema and rows, rather than copying low-level database files. The key benefit is portability: logical backups can be restored across minor and sometimes major PostgreSQL versions, inspected in a text editor, and selectively applied. For example, a plain S Q L dump shows CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements, which you can read to audit schema changes. However, logical backups can be slower for very large data sets and may require different strategies for performance. A common misconception is that logical backups replace physical backups — they do not. Physical backups capture the exact on-disk state and are required for point-in-time recovery. Use logical backups when you need portability, auditing, selective restores, or schema migration. As a practical rule, combine logical and physical backups in your strategy: logical for portability and selective needs, and physical for fast full recovery and point-in-time requirements. Consider the restore path when you select a logical format so you always know how recovery will proceed.

Let's walk through the basic pg_dump invocation and what each part does. A typical simple command is pg_dump -U postgres mydatabase > mydatabase_backup. sql. The -U option specifies the user for the connection; depending on your authentication method you may be prompted for a password. The database name tells pg_dump which single database to export; remember pg_dump operates per database and will not export cluster-level objects. The greater-than symbol redirects the standard output of pg_dump into a file. This plain-text S Q L script contains CREATE and INSERT or COPY statements and is easily inspected and edited. Use this form for small databases or when you need to audit schema changes. A misconception is thinking redirection always creates a portable binary; it produces a readable S Q L file and may be slow for very large datasets. If you need parallel restores or selective object recovery later, prefer custom or directory formats. Practice: create a small sample database, run the command, open the produced S Q L script, and confirm the presence of CREATE statements. This exercise reinforces what is captured and how you would restore it using psql.

pg_dump supports multiple output formats, and choosing the right one affects your restore options and performance. The plain text format produces a S Q L script and is easy to inspect and edit, making it useful for audits or cross-version compatibility. The custom format is compressed and flexible; it is the recommended general-purpose format because pg_restore can selectively restore objects and run multiple jobs in parallel. Tar format creates an archive similar to custom but is slightly less flexible; you can still extract components with pg_restore. The directory format generates a directory with one file per table and a table-of-contents file. Directory format shines on very large databases because you can dump and restore in parallel using --jobs. A common mistake is using plain format for large datasets; restoring becomes slow and stressful. If you expect to restore specific tables or benefit from parallelism, choose custom (-F c) or directory (-F d). For small databases or when you must hand-edit S Q L, plain format remains appropriate. Consider your restore scenarios when picking a format so backups match your recovery needs.

Custom and directory formats unlock selective restore and parallelism. Create a custom archive with pg_dump -F c -f mydb. custom mydatabase. This file is compressed and contains a table of contents that pg_restore can read. To restore a custom archive, use pg_restore and you can select specific tables or schema elements, and specify parallel jobs where supported. The directory format uses -F d and writes a folder with one file per table plus a TOC file; this layout is ideal for running pg_dump or pg_restore with --jobs to exploit multiple CPUs. For example, use pg_dump -F d -f /tmp/mydb_dir mydatabase and later pg_restore -j 4 -d targetdb /tmp/mydb_dir to restore using four jobs. A common misconception is that --jobs speeds up plain S Q L dumps — it does not; parallel jobs work only with custom and directory formats. When dealing with very large tables, the directory format may simplify partial recovery because individual table files are separate. Always test restores locally to confirm that parallel restore orders and dependency resolutions succeed, and remember that pg_dump with jobs reduces wall-clock time but still requires sufficient input and output throughput.

pg_dump includes many options to control which parts of a database you export. --schema-only produces only DDL statements such as CREATE TABLE and CREATE INDEX, which is useful when migrating schema or creating a development environment without data. --data-only exports table data without DDL; this is valuable when you already have the schema in place and need to populate data. --clean adds DROP commands before CREATE statements so restores can start from a clean state; --create includes a CREATE DATABASE statement so the dump can recreate the database itself. The --inserts and --column-inserts options force insertion via INSERT statements rather than COPY; these are safer for older server compatibility or differing column orders but are much slower. Use --exclude-table or --exclude-schema to omit parts of the database you don't want included. A common misconception is that --data-only will always restore faster — performance depends on method: COPY is usually faster than INSERT. Choose options based on the restore scenario: schema migrations, data refreshes, or selective table transfers. Practice by creating schema-only and data-only dumps and restoring them to a prepared target to confirm behavior.

It’s important to understand the limits of pg_dump: it backs up a single database’s schema and data but does not capture cluster-wide global objects. Global objects include roles (users), tablespaces, and database definitions themselves. If you only back up individual databases with pg_dump, you may miss role definitions and tablespace definitions that are required when restoring into a new instance. This omission can cause restore failures or require manual re-creation of those objects. To capture global objects, use pg_dumpall, which outputs a plain-text S Q L script that contains CREATE ROLE and CREATE TABLESPACE statements followed by per-database dumps. A common mistake is relying solely on pg_dump archives and neglecting roles; after a crash, restoring databases without recreating roles can leave ownership and privileges broken. Therefore, include a pg_dumpall export in your backup plan for cluster metadata. For selective restores, still rely on per-database pg_dump archives, but keep a recent pg_dumpall for global state so you can reconstitute the instance accurately in disaster recovery. What pg_dump does not include means pg_dump omits cluster global objects; use pg_dumpall to capture roles, tablespaces, and database definitions for full instance recovery.. In practical terms, global objects and why pg_dumpall is necessary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

pg_dumpall produces a plain-text S Q L script that represents the entire cluster, including global objects. A typical command is pg_dumpall -U postgres > full_cluster_backup. sql. The output begins with CREATE ROLE and CREATE TABLESPACE statements, then includes CREATE DATABASE commands and per-database dumps. This single file is convenient for capturing the full instance state, but it can be large and difficult to edit if you only need a subset of objects. If you must restore specific parts from a pg_dumpall script, you may need to manually extract sections, which is error-prone. The recommended approach is to keep per-database pg_dump archives for recovery of individual databases, and maintain a pg_dumpall export to capture the global configuration that pg_dump omits. During recovery, restore the pg_dumpall script first to recreate roles and tablespaces, then restore individual database archives. A common misconception is that pg_dumpall replaces per-database backups — it does not. Plan your backup sequence and test it in a staging environment to validate the order and completeness of restores. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Administrators commonly make avoidable mistakes when creating logical backups. The first frequent error is assuming pg_dump includes global objects; without pg_dumpall you may miss roles and tablespaces. To prevent this, schedule a pg_dumpall alongside per-database pg_dump archives and test restores to ensure roles and ownership map correctly. Second, choosing the wrong format for the use case — using plain format for very large databases — can cause slow restores; choose custom or directory formats for parallelism and selective restores. Third, not testing restores or storing backups on the same server exposes you to single-point failures; always store backups off-host and perform restore drills. Fourth, using --inserts indiscriminately can severely slow restoration; prefer COPY-based dumps unless compatibility requires INSERT statements. Finally, forgetting permissions on backup files can allow unauthorized access; set restrictive permissions and consider encryption. For each mistake, there is a prevention step: include pg_dumpall, choose appropriate formats, store backups off-site, test restores often, and secure backup files.
